newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-UK academic fears German grip on Europe.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-UK academic fears German grip on Europe.

text.p: German influence over the development of the European Union is likely to grow in the next century, steering Europe increasingly towards a centralised system of government, Brussels-based academic John Laughland says.
In a recent interview, Laughland, who opposes plans for dissolving European nation states in favour of full union, said he reckons German ambitions go beyond well being part of unified Europe.
"Germany like any normal country is trying to increase its power. It would be completely naive and absurd to believe that somehow it is acting for altruistic motives," he said.
Laughland, a fiercely-Eurosceptic commentator for several newspapers, believes Germany's grip on Europe is founded on the country's undeniable economic clout.

He believes it has also succeeded in persuading its allies to adopt its vision of supranational institutions -- including a Bundesbank-type central bank -- governing an ever-closer grouping of states.

Laughland comments contrast this week with growing evidence that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition is stumbling over plans to impose the toughest possible conditions for a single European currency -- conditions which even Germany may struggle to meet by 1999.

But Laughland sees the whole EMU debate as evidence of Germany's over-riding influence in Europe and the centralising trend it supports which, he thinks, will stifle debate over what direction Europe should take.

"If you transfer power to supranational institutions that are remote from nation states, you create a superstate which people will feel even more alienated from than they already feel from national bodies."

Post-war anxiety about a resurgent Germany has fuelled opposition to a united Europe in the last two decades, reinforced by complaints that Germany's economic muscle has given it disproportionate leverage.

The economic statistics speak for themselves -- Germany's share of the EU's GDP in 1996 was over 28 percent, compared with 18 percent for runner-up France and 13 percent each for Britain and Italy, Economist Intelligence Unit data shows. And the mark remains the second most important reserve currency after the dollar.

Laughland, who recently published a book 'The Tainted Source' criticising what he sees as plans to create an "illiberal, centralised" European superstate, says that many of the other European partners have bowed to the inevitable and let Germany set the pace.
"Even those European powers which wanted to dilute the influence of the Bundesbank have ended up with a system that extends it not dilutes it," Laughland said.

While Chancellor Kohl has indicated he wants a single European currency to rein in the mark's dominance, Laughland instead fears Germany's sway over EMU sets a dangerous precedent for the 15-nation bloc.
"French and other politicians no longer advocate the leftist argument that the EU needs a central bank to get an easier monetary policy to help the unemployed.
"What they're saying is: 'We need a strong currency, low interest rates and low inflation -- in other words what we need is the deutschemark'", Laughland said.
He cites the ongoing dispute between Germany and Italy about whether Italy should be in the first wave of monetary union in 1999 as evidence of its power of veto.
"Germany wants to control the hard-core," he said. "And if they want one thing its that the Italians stay out of it."

The dispute recently prompted Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, defending Italy's right to join EMU in 1999, to voice a much-whispered fear that: "Europe is not just about a currency...German culture cannot represent by itself all of Europe."

Laughland attributes modern Germany's enthusiasm for a fully-integrated Europe to a German creed prevalent in the last 60 years, initiated by the National Socialist movement, which believes the nation-state should be replaced by something bigger.
Behind its determination to join forces with its European partners, however, the British academic detects deep, historically-founded anxieties.
"German politicians say there is no alternative to European integration because if it fails, they think 'sooner or later the other countries in Europe will unite against us'", Laughland said.
